parts.model: At 0 °C ice and liquid water are at the melting and freezing point, so they coexist. Some molecules also leave both the ice and the liquid as water vapor (sublimation and evaporation). Solid, liquid and gas are all present.

parts.prompt: Describe the spacing, motion and organization of the particles in a solid, a liquid and a gas of the same substance.
parts.model: Solid: close together in fixed positions, vibrating, most organized. Liquid: close together but able to slide past each other, less organized. Gas: far apart, moving fast and randomly, least organized.

parts.prompt: What happens to particle motion as a substance is cooled toward 0 K, and why can it not be cooled below 0 K?
parts.model: The particles move more and more slowly. At 0 K (-273.15 °C) they have the minimum possible motion, so there is no lower temperature. That is why 0 K is absolute zero.

parts.prompt: Name the change of state for each and say whether energy is added or removed: ice to water, steam to water, water to ice, dry ice to gas, frost forming on a window.
parts.model: Ice to water: melting, energy added. Steam to water: condensation, energy removed. Water to ice: freezing, energy removed. Dry ice to gas: sublimation, energy added. Frost forming: deposition, energy removed.

questions.title: Test-style FRQ 2: Colloids
questions.stem: A food truck sells several colloids. Whipped cream and mayonnaise are made, hair spray is sprayed from a can, marshmallows are served and gelatin dessert is chilled. A sign beside the truck says "FOG WARNING" because a smoke machine is running.

parts.prompt: Give the structure (what is dispersed in what) and the colloid name for whipped cream, mayonnaise, hair spray mist, marshmallow and gelatin dessert.
parts.model: Whipped cream: gas in a liquid, foam. Mayonnaise: liquid in a liquid, emulsion. Hair spray mist: liquid in a gas, aerosol. Marshmallow: gas in a solid, solid sol. Gelatin dessert: liquid in a solid, gel.

parts.prompt: Smoke from the machine and fog from the same machine are both colloids with the same name. Give the name and the structure of each.
parts.model: Both are aerosols. Smoke is a solid dispersed in a gas; fog is a liquid dispersed in a gas.

parts.prompt: Describe an experiment that shows the mayonnaise is a colloid and not a solution.
parts.model: Shine a light beam through a dilute sample. If it is a colloid the particles scatter the light and the beam is visible (Tyndall effect); a solution does not scatter the beam.

parts.prompt: Compare a colloid, a solution and a suspension on particle size and settling.
parts.model: A solution has the smallest particles and does not settle or scatter light. A colloid has particles about 1 to 1000 nm, is stable, does not settle on standing and scatters light. A suspension has large particles that settle upon standing.

questions.title: Test-style FRQ 3: Defining the liquids
questions.stem: In another lab, Liquid X is pale yellow, thin and smells like lemon. It has a density of 0.85 g/mL and a pH of 3.1, and its data sheet says it reacts with metals and with bases. Liquid Y is colorless and has no odor. It has a density of 1.00 g/mL and a pH of 7.0, and its data sheet says it does not react with metals. When X and Y are mixed in a flask, the mixture fizzes, the temperature rises from 21 °C to 27 °C, and a white solid settles out.

parts.prompt: List the physical properties you can see in the description.
parts.model: Liquid X: pale yellow, thin, lemon smell, density 0.85 g/mL. Liquid Y: colorless, no odor, density 1.00 g/mL.

parts.prompt: List the chemical properties you can see in the description.
parts.model: Liquid X: pH 3.1 (acidic), reacts with metals, reacts with bases. Liquid Y: pH 7.0 (neutral) and does not react with metals.

parts.prompt: Decide whether mixing X and Y is a physical or chemical change and give three pieces of evidence.
parts.model: Chemical change. Evidence: fizzing (a gas was given off), a temperature change from 21 °C to 27 °C (+6 °C), and a white solid (precipitate) formed.

parts.prompt: Is density an intensive or extensive property? Explain with Liquid X.
parts.model: Intensive. Density does not depend on the amount: 10 mL or 1 L of Liquid X still has a density of 0.85 g/mL. Mass and volume are extensive.

questions.title: Test-style FRQ 4: Putting it in order
questions.stem: A student is organizing thoughts from the chapter. Answer each comparison.

parts.prompt: What is the difference between a solute, a solvent and a solution? Use sugar water as the example.
parts.model: In sugar water the solvent (water) does the dissolving, the solute (sugar) is dissolved, and the solution is the mixture of the two.

parts.prompt: Compare and contrast intensive and extensive physical properties with an example of each.
parts.model: Both are physical properties observed without changing the substance. An intensive property is always true for the substance whatever the amount (density, color, boiling point); an extensive property depends on the amount of matter (mass, volume, length).

parts.prompt: Compare and contrast a solution and a suspension.
parts.model: Both are mixtures. A solution is homogeneous and does not settle (salt water); a suspension is heterogeneous and settles upon standing (mud, juice with pulp, oil and water).

parts.prompt: Compare and contrast evaporation and distillation.
parts.model: Both boil off a liquid and are physical. Evaporation lets the liquid escape as a gas to leave a solid behind; distillation traps and condenses the vapor to collect the liquid.

parts.prompt: Compare and contrast synthesis and decomposition reactions.
parts.model: Both are chemical changes that make new substances. In synthesis two or more substances combine to form something new; in decomposition one substance breaks down into two or more.

sections.name: Day 2: T/F, Labeling, MCQ
examTips: The real Day 2 has 8 true/false, 2 labeling questions and about 13 multiple choice. This section mirrors that order.
Turn the Timer on and check answers at the end to match test conditions. Use Flag for review on hard ones.
tips: Read every choice before you pick one, then cross off the ones you can prove wrong with the red X.
Hard questions often mix up near-neighbors: element versus molecule, compound versus mixture, physical change versus chemical change. Decide which pair the question is testing.
For formula codes, look for an & first (mixture). Then count capital letters: one means an element, two or more means a compound.
When data is given (masses, bubbles, a leftover solid), say what the data shows before you look at the choices.
Watch extreme words such as "only," "always," "never" and "all." They are usually wrong.

questions.stem: A heterogeneous mixture can be separated by physical methods.
questions.exp: Every mixture can be separated into its pure substances by physical means.

questions.stem: Flammability is a chemical property.
questions.exp: Flammability describes the ability to burn, which forms new substances.

questions.stem: A compound has the same composition no matter where the sample came from.
questions.exp: A compound always has the same combination of atoms.

questions.stem: Boiling point is an extensive property.
questions.exp: Boiling point does not depend on the amount, so it is intensive.

questions.stem: In a chemical change, atoms are rearranged to form new substances.
questions.exp: Bonds are broken and re-formed, so the products differ from the starting substances.

questions.stem: A drawing of one lone atom is enough to prove the sample is an element.
questions.exp: A single atom could be a tiny piece of a mixture. You need to see the other particles in the sample.

questions.stem: A beam of light is visible in a colloid but not in a true solution.
questions.exp: Colloid particles scatter light (the Tyndall effect). Solution particles are too small to do that.

questions.stem: Whipped cream is an emulsion because it contains a liquid.
questions.exp: Whipped cream is gas bubbles in a liquid, which is a foam. An emulsion is a liquid in a liquid.

questions.stem: Label each material as an element, a compound or a mixture.

items.exp: One capital letter, one type of atom.
Potassium and bromine bonded in one formula.
The & separates two different substances (two elements).
Hydrogen and oxygen in a different ratio than water: still one compound.
Eight sulfur atoms bonded, only one type of atom.
Two compounds sitting together.

questions.stem: Label each change as a physical change or a chemical change.

items.exp: Only the state changes.
A gas forms as a new substance.

items.t: Cutting a piece of paper in half
items.exp: Size changes but not composition.
Burning forms new substances and releases energy.
The salt keeps its identity and can be recovered.

items.t: A cut apple slice turning brown
items.exp: The apple reacts with oxygen in the air and forms new substances.

questions.stem: A liquid and a gas are each in a sealed 500 mL container. Which observation distinguishes the liquid?
options: It takes the shape of the container and fills all 500 mL.
It has a definite volume that can be less than 500 mL.
Its particles are far apart and move randomly.
Its particles are locked into rigid positions.
questions.exp: A liquid has a definite volume and takes the shape of its container without filling it.
why: That describes a gas; a liquid fills only the volume it has.
This describes a gas.
This describes a solid.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a chemical change?
options: Alcohol evaporating from your skin
A glass bottle shattering on the floor
A silver spoon tarnishing in air
Butter softening on a warm counter
questions.exp: Tarnish is a new substance formed when silver reacts with substances in the air.
why: Evaporation is a change of state, a physical change.
Breaking glass only changes shape and size.
Softening is a physical change.

questions.stem: Which list contains one element, one compound and one mixture, in that order?
options: H₂O, Br₂, Cu & Zn
N₂, N₂ & O₂, NO₂
CO, Co, C₆H₁₂O₆ & H₂O
Au, CO₂, NaCl & H₂O
questions.exp: Au is an element, CO₂ is a compound and NaCl & H₂O is a mixture.
why: The order is compound, element, mixture.
The order is element, mixture, compound.
The order is compound, element, mixture.

questions.stem: Which separation depends on a difference in boiling point?
options: Collecting pure water from salt water in a condenser
Separating ink pigments on a strip of absorbent paper
Leaving a puddle of salt water to sit in the sun
Removing sand from water with a piece of filter paper
questions.exp: Distillation boils the component with the lower boiling point and condenses it.
why: This depends on adherence to a surface.
This is evaporation, which relies on volatility.
This depends on state or particle size.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT matter?
options: Helium gas inside a party balloon
A beam of light from a flashlight
Steam rising from a boiling kettle
Dust floating in the flashlight beam
questions.exp: Light has no mass and does not take up space like matter does.
why: Helium has mass and volume.
Steam is water in the gas state.
Dust has mass and takes up space.

questions.stem: A white solid disappears when stirred into water. Which finding best shows it dissolved instead of reacting?
options: Gas bubbles leave the liquid as it is being stirred.
The liquid turns a color that neither substance had before.
Evaporating the water leaves the original solid behind.
The beaker becomes warm and a new solid forms in it.
questions.exp: Recovering the original solid shows it did not become a new substance, so the change was physical.
why: Bubbles point toward a chemical change.
A new color points toward a chemical change.
Heat and a new solid point toward a chemical change.

questions.stem: Which drawing best represents a sample of an element?
options: One single atom shown all by itself in the drawing
Separate atoms of two different kinds mixed together
Two different atoms bonded together into pairs
Many identical atoms, none of a different kind
questions.exp: Many identical particles with one type of atom show a pure substance made of one element.
why: A lone atom could come from a mixture; more of the sample is needed.
Two kinds of atom would be a mixture.
Bonded different atoms would be a compound.

questions.stem: Which result of electrolysis best shows that water is a compound?
options: Two different gases form from one pure substance.
The volume of liquid water slowly increases over time.
The water gets hot as the current passes through it.
Bubbles appear near each electrode as current flows.
questions.exp: A compound can be broken into simpler substances, here hydrogen and oxygen.
why: The liquid does not increase; gas forms as the water is used up.
Heat does not show composition.
Bubbles alone do not show that the substance is a compound.

questions.stem: Which formula represents a mixture of an element and a compound?
options: H₂ & O₂
O₂ & H₂O
CO₂
NaCl & KBr
questions.exp: O₂ is an element and H₂O is a compound, joined by an &.
why: Both are elements.
There is no & here, so this is one compound.
Both are compounds.

questions.stem: A student watches a tea light burn for 20 minutes. Which observation best shows a chemical change?
options: The wax near the wick turned to liquid and then pooled around it.
The wax became a little softer as the candle burned down.
A flame formed and wax was used up, giving off heat and light.
The candle was warm to the touch after twenty minutes.
questions.exp: Burning wax reacts with oxygen to form new substances and releases heat and light.
why: Melting is physical.
Softening is a physical change.
Warmth alone is weak evidence of a new substance.

questions.stem: Steel wool is heated until it glows inside a sealed flask that contains air. What happens to the total mass of the sealed flask?
options: It increases because oxygen combined with the iron.
It decreases because the iron burned away.
It increases because heat added mass.
It stays the same because nothing entered or left.
questions.exp: In a sealed flask the oxygen that joins the iron is already inside, so the total mass is unchanged.
why: The oxygen came from inside the flask, so the total mass stays the same.
Nothing left the sealed flask.
Heat is not matter.

questions.stem: Which pair of structures is correctly matched with a colloid name that is used for both?
options: Solid in a gas and liquid in a gas: aerosol
Solid in a liquid and liquid in a solid: sol
Gas in a liquid and liquid in a liquid: foam
Solid in a gas and gas in a solid: aerosol
questions.exp: Aerosol is used for both solid in a gas (smoke) and liquid in a gas (fog).
why: A sol is only a solid in a liquid. A liquid in a solid is a gel.
These are two different colloids: foam and emulsion.
Gas in a solid is a solid sol, not an aerosol.

questions.stem: A mixture does not settle on standing, cannot be removed by a simple filter, and makes a flashlight beam visible. What is it?
options: A solution
A colloid
A suspension
A pure compound
questions.exp: Staying mixed, passing through filters and scattering light are all properties of a colloid.
why: A solution would not scatter the beam.
A suspension settles on standing.
A compound is not a mixture.
